done.why: After a few minutes I was in a stalemate duel with a hooded figure who mirrors me and won't finish me. It had no clear goal and I wasn't pulled further in.

about: A dream-like final test below an endless stair. You take the lantern, find an Elvish sword in a rock, and meet a hooded figure who fights exactly as you do. It seems to be a duel against yourself, set by a silver-haired old man who wants you to prove yourself worthy.

moments.note: The sword wouldn't come out of the rock, then appeared in my hand when I entered the shadow land.
I took two serious wounds in a row and was nearly dead after a few exchanges, with no warning.
The figure disarmed me and handed the sword back like a teacher. That was a nice touch.
The fight dragged on with no sense of progress or what winning would mean.

wished: A clearer sense of what the goal is.
A way to see whether I was winning the duel.
More to explore before the fight started.

lines.line: It could end this. Instead it stoops, picks up your sword, and gives it back to you hilt first, the way a teacher does.
lines.why: It turned the fight into something with character and hinted the opponent is a teacher.

lines.line: A fight that is going badly can be walked away from, into the dark, where it will not follow; wounds mend with time, on both sides, and the figure will be here when you come back for it.
lines.why: A useful hint that I could retreat and heal, which changed how I read the danger.

fun.why: The opening was intriguing, but the combat was repetitive attack-spam.

engagement.why: I quit within about 13 turns because nothing kept pulling me forward.

difficulty.why: I was nearly dead within four exchanges, but the opponent then declined to kill me, so the danger felt uneven.

interestingness.why: The mirror-opponent and teacher idea is interesting, and the dream framing at the start sets a tone.

prose.why: The prose is atmospheric and the combat narration is varied and characterful.
